text:
“Perhaps from my parents, perhaps...” she added hesitantly, “from my brother.”

“And not from me, in any case?”

“From you? How from you?”

“You once told me, while speaking to me of other things: ‘My family bores me; perhaps a day will come when I shall be free, entirely free, because I want to sing.’ Do you remember telling me that?”

“Yes, I remember, and I repeat: A day will come, perhaps soon, when I shall be free.”

“There, and thinking of that day, I too had a dream... but one so beautiful that I dare not tell it to you.”

“Dreams...” she joked, “dreams have this good thing about them: they serve to tell things that are too difficult to say.”

“You are right, Loretta,” he admitted. “Then, a dream. That I should get you a little villa, not too far from Villa Giuliani, small, for you alone. A hidden little villa, with a beautiful garden, an orchard, a stable. You would be free; no one would know who you are. Sometimes, so as not to remain alone, you would open the gate for me.”

“Ah... and that is the dream?”

“Yes, that is it.”

She reflected for a moment, then said:

“Go on.”

“What do you mean?”

“After the summer...”

“Well, after the summer you will be able to choose whatever you like. In autumn, for example, a beautiful journey, a little getaway, by motorcar, if you wish, even abroad, if you wish... And in winter, your house in the city, a lady companion to preserve appearances, a teacher to teach you singing.”

“And in spring,” she exclaimed, still tempted, “since the year blooms again, another is put in Lora’s place, and everything begins again: the same villa, the journey, the house in the city... No, thank you!”

“Another? But what are you saying? Have you still not understood that I love you, that I have loved you for many months, more strongly every day? That you can make me obey like a child, and that you alone, you alone, must give me back the peace I no longer have?... Another? That word has no meaning! But think for a moment. Do you believe I do not know what risks I am running by making you this proposal? Well, what do I care? I do not want to, I can no longer think! No danger frightens me. Only say yes to me! Ask me for whatever you want, but say yes to me!”

“I am not asking for anything,” she said, regretting that she had allowed herself to appear so calculating.

“Then listen, listen to me...” And he knelt before her armchair and encircled her with his arms.

“What are you doing? What are you doing?”

“Nothing; I am begging you on my knees. Care for me a little; be good to me for once!”

Thus on his knees, leaning toward her in the ardor of his desire, with passionate eyes and a pleading voice, Rafa was almost handsome, and she looked at him.

“Come, leave me alone...” she said, with a certain annoyance.

He held her tightly around the waist and, leaning on her a little, covered her dress and her wrists with tiny kisses.

“How many mistresses have you had sit in this armchair?” she asked suddenly.

“How many? None.”

“Oh, come now! I am asking out of curiosity.”

“Perhaps,” he said, “some woman has come here, but I do not remember. They were not mistresses; they were not you. If you do not like it, we shall change houses. I had no love before I met you. Now you seem the first to me. I love you, I love you in every way; you persecute me and you please me. You are beautiful. You have such an indefinable grace that I suffer when I am near you. Be good to me; do not laugh!...”

She was indeed laughing, but with a somewhat nervous laugh, and her mouth, her eyes, her hands were no longer so calm.

“No, leave me alone...” she pleaded. “Let me go, please... you are hurting me terribly...”

In the half-light he saw her turn pale; he hid his face in her lap, and with his arms he clasped her knees.

She tried to lift his burning forehead, tried to push away that troublesome mouth, but, unable to overcome his strength, with sudden anger she thrust her convulsed fingers into his hair.

Then the struggle was brief: desperately, the girl closed her eyes and let herself be carried away...

But she saw another room, at night, with its windows open above a lake white with moonlight, and the stars close and infinite; another man bent over her, covering her with caresses and kisses. And she saw herself again in that bed, and relived the agony of that vanished hour, and for an instant it seemed to her that he had returned, that he was there, on his knees, and was kissing her terribly as he had then, and that his hands were running feverishly, ardently, over all her tormented body, and that a mouth was rising, rising to her lips, full of anguish, fever, voluptuousness, and terror...

A little later, the adjoining room was dark, and from room to room, through the silent house, there was suddenly heard the cry of her lost virginity.




II


At about five in the afternoon, Beppe Cianella entered the Club and, after ordering an iced drink, sprawled indolently on a leather sofa near the small table where Gigi Saletta, nicknamed Saponetta, and several others were playing poker.

Beppe Cianella was hot and wiped his sweating forehead with a brightly colored silk handkerchief. He unbuttoned his waistcoat, lit a cigar, and blissfully closed his eyes as if to doze off. But it was too hot to sleep. In a still drowsy voice, Beppe Cianella called the servant and asked him to turn the fan toward him.

When the cool air struck him, he stretched out more comfortably on the sofa and, with a feeling of true bliss, tried to close his mischievous eyes.

“Rafa Giuliani is having an affair,” he said with a slight yawn.

“So much the better for him!” replied one of the players.

Sacco Berni had attempted a daring “bluff,” but Gigi Saponetta, a highly skilled player, had forced him to show his hand, and the others, laughing wildly over it, mocked the trickster who had been tricked.

Count Berrini passed by at the back, in his shirtsleeves, bellowing at the servants because he could not find a newspaper; Lello Fornara, the languishing one, was writing his daily love letter in a corner; through the open doorway leading into the billiard room, the balls could be heard striking one another amid the noisy quarrels of old Baron Gioacchini and his young pupil Leonardo Sergi.

“Rafa Giuliani is having an affair!” Beppe Cianella, who could not fall asleep, repeated between one yawn and the next.
